newsitem.title: USA: Louisiana to drop lawsuit against insurers.
newsitem.headline: Louisiana to drop lawsuit against insurers.

text.p: Louisiana Attorney General Richard Ieyoub said on Friday he expects the state to drop its lawsuit against insurers after reaching a landmark settlement with the tobacco industry.

"It appears, as a result of the settlement that we would not continue that (lawsuit) against the insurers as a result of the terms of the agreement," Ieyoub said in a telephone interview with Reuters.

Tobacco companies agreed to pay 80 percent of any proceeds they receive from their insurers to the states in addition to the $368.5 billion they agreed to pay over 25 years to compensate the states and smokers.
Louisiana in March named more than 100 insurers as defendants in a lawsuit seeking to recover medical costs related to the harmful effects of smoking.

Louisiana took action against the insurers using the state's direct action statute, which allows injured parties to file suit directly against insurers who have insured the people or businesses responsible for their injuries.
Ieyoub said the state was not dropping its action against the insurers because of any concern that it might not have a strong case.
"I think we would have an excellent case," Ieyoub said. "I believe there's coverage. I believe they (the tobacco companies) know there's coverage and I think we would be successful," he said.
But, he said, he was willing to drop the case as a concession in the wide-ranging tobacco talks.

"I think this settlement is so good and the things that we have accomplished are so huge in the way of saving lives and in the way of advancing the public health of this country, that any concessions relative to the direct action statute sort of pales," he said.
However, Ieyoub said he did not know whether the tobacco companies will pursue their insurers for coverage under their product liability policies.
But, he said, the settlement may inflict enough pain on tobacco companies to make it worth their while to at least try to get something from their insurers.
"As you can see, the tobacco companies are going to have to pay a lot, a lot, of money," he said.
The nearly $370 billion payment called for under the settlment "is a lot of money in anybody's book.
"And if, in fact, they did have coverage, it's entirely possible they would try to reimburse themselves, to some extent anyway, through their insurers," he said.
But if the tobacco companies do not seek to collect on their insurance policies or if their claims are denied, then the states would receive nothing in addition to the settlement.
The insurance industry has argued that the policies sold to tobacco companies do not cover the industry for losses related to smoking-related illnesses.
And any attempt by tobacco companies to try to collect on those policies will be bitterly fought by insurers.
In addition, Ieyoub said insurers did not participate in the states' negotiations with the tobacco industry.
Instead, Ieyoub said, as chairman of the insurance committee in the tobacco talks, he dealt with the tobacco company representatives.
After discussing the insurance matter with the tobacco companies, he said, he believes they came away "pretty much resolved in their belief that there was coverage."
